OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant), a citizen of Tunisia, and her children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in XXXX XXXX (the associate appellants) citizens of Tunisia and Libya, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject their refugee protection claims because they have an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Bizerte, Tunisia.

[2] The principal appellant's refugee protection claim is based on the allegations contained in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) of her husband, who was recognized as a Convention refugee. The principal appellant's husband alleges that he was persecuted because of his employment at the XXXX XXXX of XXXX in Tunisia. He alleges that death threats were made against him, including threats targeting the associate appellants. Fearing for his and his family member's lives, he left with the appellants to seek refuge in Canada.

[3] The principal appellant states that the RPD erred in failing to take into account the objective of family reunification, the family unit and the principle of indirect persecution. The RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims because there is an IFA available to them in Bizerte, Tunisia.

argument_evidence.context_text: [4] The determinative question for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA in Bizerte.
[5] My answer to the determinative question is no.
The RPD reasonably determined that the appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

DETERMINATION

[6] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD reasonably determined that the appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

[9] At the hearing, the principal appellant stated that the people who know her husband could track her down in Bizerte. She also raised a fear with respect to the Tunisian authorities because of her job as a XXXX XXXX in the country's largest XXXX and because she had left the country before resigning. She stated that the authorities could be suspicious of her because of her husband's past. When asked about the nature of these suspicions, the principal appellant vaguely replied to this question and was unable to explain her statement. When she was asked why her allegations regarding her fears were not in her written account, the principal appellant replied that she had tried to summarize it.4

[10] Without any evidence that these people had made such efforts since the appellants left the country, in the city of Tunis or elsewhere, the RPD considered the alleged fear to be speculative. It stated that the principal appellant's husband is no longer employed by the XXXX XXXX the source of the alleged problems, and that the appellants lived in the town of Bizerte for only a short time. With respect to the allegations left out of the written account regarding the alleged fear of the authorities, the RPD considered the principal appellant's allegations to be unreasonable because she was represented by counsel and had ample time to make changes to her written account. The RPD was of the opinion that the principal appellant failed to establish the existence of any standard requiring her to seek authorization before leaving her country, or provide any evidence that, at present, she would be a subject of interest to the authorities of her country because of her departure. It considered that the appellants failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution in Bizerte on one of the Convention grounds or a danger to their lives or a risk of torture or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. It considered that they also failed to establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for them, taking into account the conditions in Bizerte and all the circumstances of the case, including their personal situation, to seek refuge at that location.

[11] In her memorandum of appeal, the principal appellant states that the RPD erred because it confused the application of sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). She states that the RPD recognized the acts of persecution against her husband in Tunisia, but that it erred in not recognizing that the entire family was targeted. She states that the RPD did not take into account all the evidence corroborating the existence of a real fear for their lives in Tunisia. She states that the RPD's decision goes against one of the objectives of the IRPA, namely, family reunification in Canada. She states that the termination of her husband's employment at the XXXX would not automatically put a stop to the persecution against them. She states that the events which occurred after the resignation increased their fear of returning to Tunisia. She states that the RPD should have accepted their refugee protection claims on the basis of the principle of [translation] "family unity." She states that the RPD should have applied the concept of indirect persecution. She states that the RPD should have considered how close Libya and Tunisia are, as well as the cultural homogeneity between Libyans and Tunisians. She states that she and her children can personally claim refugee status by reason of their membership in a particular social group, namely, that of women. She states that there is no viable IFA for them in Tunisia because of the persecution against them.

[12] Before examining the issue of the IFA and addressing the concepts of family unity and indirect persecution, I note the following as stated in Akinfolajimi:5

[5] I am mindful that the effect of the RPD decision is the separation of the family. However, the IRPA objective of family unification is one of a number of objectives the IRPA seeks to advance over a wide variety of contexts. It is not a governing factor when determining if an individual claimant is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97. Instead the IRPA provides other mechanisms that address the objective of family unification, mechanisms that might well be available to the applicants.
. . .

[30] As discussed at the outset of this Judgment, family unification is a stated objective of the IRPA and decisions within the IRPA context that lead to a different result are unquestionably difficult. However protection claims must be assessed individually and on their own merit on the basis of the definitions set out in sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

[13] With respect to indirect persecution, the case law clearly states that this does not amount to persecution within the meaning of the Convention.6 It was stated that the persons claiming refugee protection must have a well-founded fear of persecution and not simply be the unwilling spectators of persecution against others.7

[14] Family as a "social group" basis for seeking Convention refugee status is based on the evidence of persecution of the family as a social group and not on the principle of family unity. It requires evidence that, by reason of membership in a family, individuals may have a well-founded fear of persecution in the future if they are forced to return to their country of origin.8

[15] It was also stated that a person cannot be considered a refugee simply because a member of their family is being persecuted and that refugee protection claimants must establish that they were targeted by agents of persecution personally or as members of a community.9

subthemes.text:
[18] I would like to point out that the principal appellant's husband is a citizen of Libya and that his refugee protection claim was examined based on his fear in that country. The principal appellant, on the other hand, is a citizen of Tunisia. Her children (the associate appellants) hold dual citizenship in Tunisia and Libya. Since the RPD considered the IFA to be a determinative question and since the associate appellants are Tunisian citizens, they must, along with the principal appellant, establish the lack of an IFA in Bizerte, the town proposed by the RPD.
Prongs of the internal flight alternative

[19] The test for IFA was developed in the case law in Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu.11 As per the case law, determining whether or not an IFA exists in a refugee protection claimant's country of origin involves a two-pronged analysis. The RAD must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the appellants would not be subjected to the risks set out in section 97 of the IRPA or that there is no serious possibility of persecution of the appellants in the proposed IFA. The situation in the proposed IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, having regard to all the circumstances, including those particular to the appellants, for them to seek refuge there.

[20] Regarding the IFA, when the principal appellant was asked about her fear if she were to settle with her children in Bizerte, she stated that the people who allegedly threatened her husband could track her down in that region. However, I note that the principal appellant's written account contains no mention of this. Just like the RPD, I am of the opinion that the principal appellant's allegations are based on suppositions not supported by any independent proof whatsoever. The principal appellant's husband's employment at the XXXX is the source of the alleged problems. But he is no longer employed by the XXXX and he therefore failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the people threatening him would track down the principal appellant in Bizerte.

[21] Furthermore, at the hearing the principal appellant raised a new alleged fear of the Tunisian authorities because of her resignation. She stated that she could be suspected by the authorities, but failed to provide further information when she was asked about this by the RPD. I would like to point out that the principal appellant is not disputing the RPD's conclusion regarding the allegations left out of her written account and I see no error in this conclusion, which I consider to be correct.

[22] With respect to the second prong of the IFA test, the audio recording revealed that the principal appellant stated that her parents live in Bizerte and that they have had no problems in relation to the allegations in her refugee protection claim. Apart from her alleged fear, the principal appellant was unable to identify other reasons she could not return to Tunisia with her children to settle in Bizerte.12 Furthermore, I would like to point out that the principal appellant presented additional written submissions13 after the hearing, but failed to provide explanations regarding the second prong of the IFA. There is no evidence to suggest that the principal appellant could not find employment or a place to live in Bizerte. She is an educated person and was previously employed for several years in Tunisia. Overall, I am of the opinion that there is an IFA for the female appellants in the location proposed by the RPD. That being said, it is not necessary for me to address the associated appellants' fear in Libya.

[23] Lastly, the RPD stated that it is aware of the documentary evidence on the situation of women in Tunisia. It stated that the principal appellant did not allege, and also failed to establish, a link between the more difficult realities of this situation and her own situation or that of her children. This conclusion is not being challenged; I examined it, while taking into account the aforementioned Guidelines, and I am of the opinion that it is correct.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant), a citizen of Tunisia, and her children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in XXXX XXXX (the associate appellants) citizens of Tunisia and Libya, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject their refugee protection claims because they have an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Bizerte, Tunisia.

[2] The principal appellant's refugee protection claim is based on the allegations contained in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) of her husband, who was recognized as a Convention refugee. The principal appellant's husband alleges that he was persecuted because of his employment at the XXXX XXXX of XXXX in Tunisia. He alleges that death threats were made against him, including threats targeting the associate appellants. Fearing for his and his family member's lives, he left with the appellants to seek refuge in Canada.

[3] The principal appellant states that the RPD erred in failing to take into account the objective of family reunification, the family unit and the principle of indirect persecution. The RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims because there is an IFA available to them in Bizerte, Tunisia.
[4] The determinative question for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA in Bizerte.

[5] My answer to the determinative question is no. I consider the RPD's decision to be correct.
DETERMINATION
[6] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD reasonably determined that the appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
ANALYSIS

[7] My role is to review all the evidence and determine whether the RPD decision is correct.1 Based on Huruglica and Rozas del Solar and after conducting my own analysis of the case, in particular by listening to the audio recording of the hearing and considering all the evidence, I am of the opinion that the correctness standard of review must be applied here.

[8] I would like to point out that, in these reasons, I considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 3: Child Refugee Claimants: Procedural and Evidentiary Issues2 and Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.3
Internal flight alternative ? Bizerte

[9] At the hearing, the principal appellant stated that the people who know her husband could track her down in Bizerte. She also raised a fear with respect to the Tunisian authorities because of her job as a XXXX XXXX in the country's largest XXXX and because she had left the country before resigning. She stated that the authorities could be suspicious of her because of her husband's past. When asked about the nature of these suspicions, the principal appellant vaguely replied to this question and was unable to explain her statement. When she was asked why her allegations regarding her fears were not in her written account, the principal appellant replied that she had tried to summarize it.4

[10] Without any evidence that these people had made such efforts since the appellants left the country, in the city of Tunis or elsewhere, the RPD considered the alleged fear to be speculative. It stated that the principal appellant's husband is no longer employed by the XXXX XXXX the source of the alleged problems, and that the appellants lived in the town of Bizerte for only a short time. With respect to the allegations left out of the written account regarding the alleged fear of the authorities, the RPD considered the principal appellant's allegations to be unreasonable because she was represented by counsel and had ample time to make changes to her written account. The RPD was of the opinion that the principal appellant failed to establish the existence of any standard requiring her to seek authorization before leaving her country, or provide any evidence that, at present, she would be a subject of interest to the authorities of her country because of her departure. It considered that the appellants failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution in Bizerte on one of the Convention grounds or a danger to their lives or a risk of torture or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. It considered that they also failed to establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for them, taking into account the conditions in Bizerte and all the circumstances of the case, including their personal situation, to seek refuge at that location.

[11] In her memorandum of appeal, the principal appellant states that the RPD erred because it confused the application of sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). She states that the RPD recognized the acts of persecution against her husband in Tunisia, but that it erred in not recognizing that the entire family was targeted. She states that the RPD did not take into account all the evidence corroborating the existence of a real fear for their lives in Tunisia. She states that the RPD's decision goes against one of the objectives of the IRPA, namely, family reunification in Canada. She states that the termination of her husband's employment at the XXXX would not automatically put a stop to the persecution against them. She states that the events which occurred after the resignation increased their fear of returning to Tunisia. She states that the RPD should have accepted their refugee protection claims on the basis of the principle of [translation] "family unity." She states that the RPD should have applied the concept of indirect persecution. She states that the RPD should have considered how close Libya and Tunisia are, as well as the cultural homogeneity between Libyans and Tunisians. She states that she and her children can personally claim refugee status by reason of their membership in a particular social group, namely, that of women. She states that there is no viable IFA for them in Tunisia because of the persecution against them.
[12] Before examining the issue of the IFA and addressing the concepts of family unity and indirect persecution, I note the following as stated in Akinfolajimi:5

[5] I am mindful that the effect of the RPD decision is the separation of the family. However, the IRPA objective of family unification is one of a number of objectives the IRPA seeks to advance over a wide variety of contexts. It is not a governing factor when determining if an individual claimant is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97. Instead the IRPA provides other mechanisms that address the objective of family unification, mechanisms that might well be available to the applicants.
. . .

[30] As discussed at the outset of this Judgment, family unification is a stated objective of the IRPA and decisions within the IRPA context that lead to a different result are unquestionably difficult. However protection claims must be assessed individually and on their own merit on the basis of the definitions set out in sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

[13] With respect to indirect persecution, the case law clearly states that this does not amount to persecution within the meaning of the Convention.6 It was stated that the persons claiming refugee protection must have a well-founded fear of persecution and not simply be the unwilling spectators of persecution against others.7

[14] Family as a "social group" basis for seeking Convention refugee status is based on the evidence of persecution of the family as a social group and not on the principle of family unity. It requires evidence that, by reason of membership in a family, individuals may have a well-founded fear of persecution in the future if they are forced to return to their country of origin.8

[15] It was also stated that a person cannot be considered a refugee simply because a member of their family is being persecuted and that refugee protection claimants must establish that they were targeted by agents of persecution personally or as members of a community.9

[16] With respect to the objective of family reunification in the IRPA,10 I am of the opinion that this is not a determinative criterion in deciding whether a person is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA. Given that the refugee protection claim of the principal appellant's husband was accepted, the IRPA provides other mechanisms to achieve the objective of family reunification. The appellants could have turned to those mechanisms.

[17] In this case, the principal appellant's written account is based on the allegations in her husband's BOC Form. There, he alleges that he was threatened because of his employment at the XXXX XXXXof XXXX in Tunisia. I would like to point out that the principal appellant's husband was recognized as a Convention refugee. While I admit that the associate appellants would have been affected by the threats against their father, the determinative question in this case is whether or not there is, for all the appellants, an IFA in Bizerte, the town proposed by the RPD.

[18] I would like to point out that the principal appellant's husband is a citizen of Libya and that his refugee protection claim was examined based on his fear in that country. The principal appellant, on the other hand, is a citizen of Tunisia. Her children (the associate appellants) hold dual citizenship in Tunisia and Libya. Since the RPD considered the IFA to be a determinative question and since the associate appellants are Tunisian citizens, they must, along with the principal appellant, establish the lack of an IFA in Bizerte, the town proposed by the RPD.
Prongs of the internal flight alternative

[19] The test for IFA was developed in the case law in Rasaratnam and Thirunavukkarasu.11 As per the case law, determining whether or not an IFA exists in a refugee protection claimant's country of origin involves a two-pronged analysis. The RAD must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the appellants would not be subjected to the risks set out in section 97 of the IRPA or that there is no serious possibility of persecution of the appellants in the proposed IFA. The situation in the proposed IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, having regard to all the circumstances, including those particular to the appellants, for them to seek refuge there.

[20] Regarding the IFA, when the principal appellant was asked about her fear if she were to settle with her children in Bizerte, she stated that the people who allegedly threatened her husband could track her down in that region. However, I note that the principal appellant's written account contains no mention of this. Just like the RPD, I am of the opinion that the principal appellant's allegations are based on suppositions not supported by any independent proof whatsoever. The principal appellant's husband's employment at the XXXX is the source of the alleged problems. But he is no longer employed by the XXXX and he therefore failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the people threatening him would track down the principal appellant in Bizerte.

[21] Furthermore, at the hearing the principal appellant raised a new alleged fear of the Tunisian authorities because of her resignation. She stated that she could be suspected by the authorities, but failed to provide further information when she was asked about this by the RPD. I would like to point out that the principal appellant is not disputing the RPD's conclusion regarding the allegations left out of her written account and I see no error in this conclusion, which I consider to be correct.

[22] With respect to the second prong of the IFA test, the audio recording revealed that the principal appellant stated that her parents live in Bizerte and that they have had no problems in relation to the allegations in her refugee protection claim. Apart from her alleged fear, the principal appellant was unable to identify other reasons she could not return to Tunisia with her children to settle in Bizerte.12 Furthermore, I would like to point out that the principal appellant presented additional written submissions13 after the hearing, but failed to provide explanations regarding the second prong of the IFA. There is no evidence to suggest that the principal appellant could not find employment or a place to live in Bizerte. She is an educated person and was previously employed for several years in Tunisia. Overall, I am of the opinion that there is an IFA for the female appellants in the location proposed by the RPD. That being said, it is not necessary for me to address the associated appellants' fear in Libya.

[23] Lastly, the RPD stated that it is aware of the documentary evidence on the situation of women in Tunisia. It stated that the principal appellant did not allege, and also failed to establish, a link between the more difficult realities of this situation and her own situation or that of her children. This conclusion is not being challenged; I examined it, while taking into account the aforementioned Guidelines, and I am of the opinion that it is correct.
CONCLUSION
[24] After examining all the evidence, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in its decision, which I consider to be correct.

[25] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the determination of the RPD that the female appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
(signed)
Toni Jedid
Me Toni Jedid
